problems.title: Climbing Stairs II
problems.problem: There are steps 0 to n. You start on step 0 with cost 0. From step i you may jump to i+1, i+2 or i+3. Landing on step j from step i costs costs[j] + (j - i)^2, where costs is 1-indexed. Find the minimum total cost to reach step n.
problems.intuition: The cheapest way to reach step j must come from one of only three places: j-1, j-2 or j-3. If we already know the cheapest cost to reach each of those, the best for j is the minimum of (best of previous step + costs[j] + jump^2). Each step only looks back three positions, so a simple left to right DP works.
approach: Create dp of size n+1, dp[0] = 0 (we start on step 0 for free).
For each step j from 1 to n, set dp[j] to infinity.
Try jump = 1, 2, 3 while j - jump >= 0: candidate = dp[j - jump] + costs[j - 1] + jump * jump (costs is 1-indexed in the statement, so step j uses costs[j - 1] in Java).
Keep the minimum candidate in dp[j].
Return dp[n]. A long array is used so no intermediate sum can overflow.

complexity.space: O(n) for dp (can be cut to O(1) by keeping only the last 3 values)

edgeCases: n = 1: only a single jump of 1 is possible.
Early steps (j = 1, 2) where some jumps would go below step 0 are skipped by the j - jump >= 0 check.
Very expensive middle steps: a jump of 3 can skip them even though it costs 9 extra.
n = 10^5 with costs 10^4: the sum stays near 10^9, computed in long to be safe.
problems.takeaway: "Reach position j from a few fixed previous positions with a cost" means 1D DP: dp[j] = min over the allowed previous states (the Min Cost Climbing Stairs / Frog Jump family).

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.problem: Given a string made of the characters ( ) [ ] { }, decide whether every bracket is closed by the same type of bracket, in the correct order, and every closing bracket has a matching opener.

examples.explanation: ( is closed by the wrong type.
( is closed before [ which was opened later, wrong order.

problems.intuition: The most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed. That is exactly Last In First Out, so a stack fits. A small trick: when we see an opener, push the closer we expect. Then a closer is valid only if it equals the top of the stack.
approach: If the length is odd, return false right away.
Scan each character.
If it is an opener, push its matching closer onto the stack.
If it is a closer, the stack must be non-empty and its popped top must equal this character; otherwise return false.
At the end, the string is valid only if the stack is empty (no unclosed openers).
dryRun: ch = ')' : closer, stack not empty, pop ')' which equals ch, continue. stack = []
End of string, stack is empty, return true.

complexity.space: O(n) for the stack in the worst case

edgeCases: Single character like "(" or "]": odd length, false.
Closer with an empty stack such as "))((": false immediately.
Only openers like "((": loop finishes but stack is not empty, false.
Deep nesting of length 10^4 works since ArrayDeque grows as needed.
problems.takeaway: Matching pairs where the latest open must close first means a stack. Pushing the expected closer keeps the comparison to a single equality check.

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.problem: A sorted array of distinct numbers may have been rotated at some unknown point, for example [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] becomes [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]. Return the index of target, or -1 if it is not there, in O(log n) time.

examples.explanation: Single element that is not the target.

problems.intuition: When you cut a rotated sorted array at mid, at least one of the two halves is still fully sorted. Comparing nums[left] with nums[mid] tells you which one. For a sorted half you can check in O(1) whether target lies inside its range, so you know which half to throw away. That keeps the normal binary search halving.
approach: left = 0, right = n - 1.
While left <= right: mid = left + (right - left) / 2. If nums[mid] == target, return mid.
If nums[left] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted: if nums[left] <= target < nums[mid], search left (right = mid - 1), else search right (left = mid + 1).
Otherwise the right half is sorted: if nums[mid] < target <= nums[right], search right (left = mid + 1), else search left (right = mid - 1).
If the loop ends, return -1.
dryRun: mid = 3, nums[3] = 7 != 0. nums[0] = 4 <= 7, left half sorted. Is 4 <= 0 < 7? No, so left = 4.
left = 4, right = 6, mid = 5, nums[5] = 1 != 0. nums[4] = 0 <= 1, left half sorted. Is 0 <= 0 < 1? Yes, so right = 4.
left = 4, right = 4, mid = 4, nums[4] = 0 == target. Return 4.
edgeCases: Single element, found or not found.
Array not rotated at all: behaves like normal binary search.
Two elements such as [3,1]: the <= in nums[left] <= nums[mid] handles left == mid.
Negative values and target at the pivot (the first element of the second run).
problems.takeaway: In a rotated sorted array, one half around mid is always sorted. Find that half, check if the target falls in its range, and discard the other half.

problems.title: Course Schedule
problems.problem: There are numCourses courses labeled 0 to numCourses - 1. A pair [a, b] means you must take b before a. Return true if it is possible to finish all courses, which is the same as asking whether the prerequisite graph has no cycle.

examples.explanation: Course 1 needs 0 and course 0 needs 1, a cycle, so it is impossible.

problems.intuition: Treat courses as nodes and draw an edge b -> a for each [a, b]. A course with no remaining prerequisites (indegree 0) can be taken now. Taking it removes its outgoing edges, which may free other courses. If we can take every course this way the graph has no cycle. Courses inside a cycle always keep indegree at least 1, so they are never taken.
approach: Build an adjacency list graph[b] containing a for each [a, b], and count indegree[a].
Push every course with indegree 0 into a queue.
Pop a course, increment taken, and decrease the indegree of each course it unlocks; when one drops to 0, push it.
When the queue is empty, return taken == numCourses.
dryRun: poll 0, taken = 1. Neighbor 1: indegree[1] becomes 0, push 1. queue = [1]
poll 1, taken = 2. No neighbors. queue empty.

complexity.time: O(V + E), V = numCourses, E = prerequisites.length
complexity.space: O(V + E) for the graph, indegree array and queue

edgeCases: No prerequisites at all: every course starts with indegree 0, true.
Self loop [0,0]: course 0 never reaches indegree 0, false.
Cycle that does not include course 0, such as 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 1: still detected because taken < numCourses.
Long chain of 2000 courses: BFS is iterative, so no stack overflow risk.
problems.takeaway: "Can all tasks with dependencies be completed?" means cycle detection in a directed graph. Kahn's algorithm (BFS on indegree 0 nodes) answers it and also gives a valid order.

problems.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
problems.problem: You are given k linked lists, each sorted in ascending order. Merge them all into one sorted linked list and return its head.

examples.explanation: The lists are 1->4->5, 1->3->4 and 2->6; merging them gives 1->1->2->3->4->4->5->6.
No lists, so the result is empty.

problems.intuition: The next node of the answer is always the smallest among the current heads of the k lists. A min-heap gives that smallest head in O(log k). After taking a node, only its own list's next node becomes a new candidate, so we push just that one. The heap never holds more than k nodes.
approach: Create a min-heap of ListNode ordered by val and push every non-null head.
Use a dummy node and a tail pointer to build the answer.
While the heap is not empty: poll the smallest node, attach it to tail, move tail forward.
If the polled node has a next node, push that next node into the heap.
Return dummy.next.
dryRun: poll 4(A), push 5(A); poll 4(B), list B is done. heap = {5(A), 6(C)}

complexity.time: O(N log k), N = total nodes, k = number of lists
complexity.space: O(k) for the heap (nodes are relinked, not copied)

edgeCases: lists is empty: heap stays empty, return null.
lists = [[]]: null heads are skipped, return null.
Some empty lists mixed with non-empty ones.
Many duplicate values across lists, and negative values.
k = 10^4 lists of one node each.
problems.takeaway: "Merge k sorted things" or "repeatedly take the smallest of k candidates" means a min-heap of size k. Divide and conquer pairwise merging is the O(1) extra space alternative with the same O(N log k) time.
